Polyuria

urine osmolality first · solute vs water diuresis · when water deprivation is indicated · desmopressin responseIs the urine dilute, and has the serum sodium already answered what the deprivation test would?

1Presentation
Bottom line
  • Urine osmolality first: under 300 is a water diuresis; 600 or more before any deprivation means the kidney concentrates, so look for solute
  • Then the sodium: high has already proven an AVP (arginine vasopressin) disorder, low means primary polydipsia; only a normal sodium needs water deprivation
  • Desmopressin after deprivation: urine concentrates in AVP deficiency, stays dilute in AVP resistance
What it is

Urine output over 3 L/day in an adult, over 2 L/day/m² in a child

Sort by

Solute or water too much drinking, too little hormone, or a kidney that ignores it

Hands off

Lithium: Lithium Therapy; a high calcium: Hypercalcemia; a sellar mass: Brain Tumors in a Child

2Urgent risks
InfantPolyuria with a high sodium in a child who cannot ask for water

If the sodium is already high, choose do not deprive; give water, then the desmopressin challenge.

The testDeprivation deliberately produces hypernatremia

If it is indicated, choose admit for supervised testing.

3Differential
Polyuria look-alikes, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Primary polydipsiaIntake drives output: psychiatric illness, or a thirst-causing drugSodium low or low-normal; urine over 600 after deprivation
AVP deficiency (central diabetes insipidus)Trauma, neurosurgery, craniopharyngioma or germinoma, a familial mutationDilute after deprivation; concentrates with desmopressin
AVP resistance (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus)Lithium, high calcium, low potassium, an inherited receptor defectDilute even after desmopressin; in a child, usually inherited
Solute (osmotic) diuresisUncontrolled diabetes or mannitolUrine osmolality 600 or more; glucose in the urine
Sickle cell trait
Polyuria and nocturia, normal sodium, low specific gravityThe trait impairs concentrating (hyposthenuria)
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH)Water retained, not lostConcentrated urine with a low sodium, and no polyuria
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Rises with desmopressinAVP deficiencyBrain MRI; desmopressin treats it
Resistance, causes excludedInherited AVP resistanceThiazide with a low-sodium diet first; indomethacin adds
On lithiumLithium-induced AVP resistanceAmiloride blocks lithium entry
Calcium high or potassium lowReversible AVP resistanceCorrect the cause first

Pause point. The bait: brain MRI or renal ultrasound before the deprivation test. Each localizes a deficiency or a resistance that has not yet been shown.

Practice
  1. 8 yo M, 2 months of polyuria and polydipsia, normal growth and neurologic examination, Na 142, glucose 100, urine specific gravity 1.001 and osmolality 120, output 3.7 L/day → Water deprivation test → a normal sodium is what leaves the diagnosis open
  2. 10 yo M with polyuria, serum Na 149 and serum osmolality 302, urine osmolality 110 → Desmopressin challenge → the deprivation endpoint has already been reached spontaneously
  3. 12 yo F whose urine osmolality stayed at 150 through deprivation and then rose to 620 after desmopressin → MRI of the brain → AVP deficiency needs its cause localized
  4. 9 yo M whose urine osmolality is 140 after deprivation and unchanged after desmopressin, with normal calcium, potassium and no medications → A thiazide with a low-sodium diet → first line once resistance is established and reversible causes are excluded
  5. 8 yo M for whom water deprivation testing has been chosen → Admit for supervised inpatient testing → the test works by producing hypernatremia deliberately
  6. 20-month-old with polyuria and a serum sodium of 148 → Water deprivation testing → severe hypernatremia in a child who cannot obtain water
  7. 14 yo M with polyuria and weight loss, urine osmolality 650, serum glucose 420, urine glucose 4+ → Osmotic diuresis → a concentrating kidney moves the problem to solute
  8. 30 yo F on an antipsychotic with polyuria, urine osmolality 90 and serum sodium 128 → Primary polydipsia → polyuria with hyponatremia needs no deprivation test
  9. Child with polyuria whose urine remains dilute when fluids are withheld → Desmopressin after water deprivation → the hormone itself is too unstable in a sample to measure routinely; serial urine osmolality is what is read
  10. 17 yo F with polyuria, constipation and a serum calcium of 12.8 → Hypercalcemia blunts the response to vasopressin → an acquired, reversible AVP resistance at the collecting duct
Pearls A sodium above 145 makes the test redundant. A sodium below normal already means primary polydipsia. Only a normal sodium calls for the test. · Serum vasopressin is rarely measured: its half-life is short and it is unstable in the sample, so the desmopressin response is the assay · AVP deficiency – the current name for central diabetes insipidus · AVP resistance – the current name for nephrogenic diabetes insipidus · Damage to the hypothalamic nuclei often makes the deficiency permanent; damage to the posterior pituitary is usually transient, because the hypothalamic neurons survive · Pregnancy can produce a transient deficiency through placental vasopressinase, secreted in its latter half · Lithium causes resistance by inhibiting aquaporin-2, and amiloride is the agent that blocks lithium's entry into the cell
Pairs with Part I Enuresis already links a very low specific gravity to diabetes insipidus and to this test. This brief covers what happens after the test is ordered. Brain Tumors in a Child covers the causes of AVP (arginine vasopressin) deficiency and the post-operative case where the diagnosis is not in doubt. Hypercalcemia covers a common, reversible acquired resistance. Ask: is the serum sodium high, low, or normal?
Transferable rule When the kidney is making dilute urine, the serum sodium shows whether a water deprivation test is still needed. A high sodium already confirms an AVP (arginine vasopressin) disorder; a low sodium already means primary polydipsia. Only a normal sodium calls for the test.
Sequencing trapMRI (magnetic resonance imaging) of the brain: the right study once a deficiency is proven, and nothing has been proven yet.
Sequencing trapRenal ultrasonography: it images the kidney, which is implicated only if desmopressin fails.
Salient decoyA BUN (blood urea nitrogen) of 30 pulls toward renal disease, but the creatinine is 1.0 and the defect is concentration, not filtration.
True-fact-wrong-slotFractional excretion of sodium: it measures perfusion, and perfusion is not in question here.
Salient decoyChest radiography: it looks for SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion), which produces concentrated urine and hyponatremia, both opposite to the findings here.
